bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body: Input cost inflation (fuel, freight); Consumer discretionary spend compression; Execution risk on store refreshes; Geopolitical uncertainty impacting global supply chains (mentioned 'Trump behavior').
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Cautiously optimistic; Operationally agile (rapid induction shift); Confident in brand equity; Prudent on pricing (only 4% hike passed to customers).
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: 78% of chain converted to electric induction woks in <2 months to hedge against LPG/PNG scarcity; Pilot testing shows 6% cost saving vs gas due to elimination of 'pilot light' wastage; April SSG surged to 11.57% immediately following store refreshes, validating the renovation thesis.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Funding history as disclosed on the journey slide: private equity raised from SAIF Partners in 2007 and Rs 176.09 crores raised through the IPO in 2012; no subsequent capital raise is mentioned.
- Franchise route used for international and select expansion: 8 of 118 units are franchisee owned and company operated, including the Dubai openings, and Chourangi in London was launched under a joint venture.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Strong portfolio of brands built over three decades, each recognised for excellence in its category, with a loyal customer base and leadership in the fine dining segment
- Strong top-of-mind recall across the Fine Dining, Casual Dining and Cloud Kitchen segments
- Multi-format portfolio spanning fine dining, casual dining, resto bars, QSR, cloud kitchens and confectioneries, allowing participation in fast-growing categories while complementing premium offerings
- Nineteenth consecutive quarter of sustained profitable growth in FY 2025-26
- Pivot to smaller and more efficient restaurant formats of around 2,000 sq. ft. that deliver faster breakeven
- Capital-light international franchise model that requires no capital expenditure from the Company while generating royalty-led earnings and limiting financial exposure to regional disruption
- Debt-free position and brand strength described as meaningful advantages in a period of elevated gas, fuel and input costs
- Growing delivery franchise supported by strategic partnerships with leading online food aggregators and delivery-optimised menus
- Brand recognition through awards during the year for Mainland China, Asia Kitchen by Mainland China, Oh! Calcutta, Sigree, Riyasat, Café Mezzuna and Sweet Bengal
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Kitchen fuel supply disruption and elevated gas and fuel prices — Management names energy supply disruption and elevated gas and fuel prices arising from the West Asia conflict as a key risk, given the industry's dependence on LPG for commercial kitchens; curtailed LNG supplies have driven up gas and fuel prices, directly raising kitchen fuel costs, threatening supply continuity for gas-dependent operations and adding freight and imported-ingredient cost pressure, with the speed of restoration of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz named as a key variable to monitor. The Company mitigates this through PNG connectivity where available, selective adoption of induction and electric cooking equipment, multi-fuel contingency planning, energy-efficient kitchen design and menu engineering; energy management is also a BRSR material issue given reliance on refrigeration, air conditioning, lighting and LPG.
- Cost of the kitchen energy transition — The accelerated shift to induction and electric cooking requires capital investment in equipment, electrical infrastructure and staff retraining, and must be balanced against the flame-based techniques integral to the Company's cuisines.
- Input cost volatility and inflation normalisation — Food inflation was unusually amiable for most of FY 2025-26 but prices are expected to normalise, and the energy crisis has revived the risk of a resurgence in commodity, fuel, packaging and logistics costs that can compress margins. The risk register also flags commodity and material price fluctuation, mitigated by advance planning of commodity supplies and evaluating hedging for select commodities.
- Dependence on the fine dining segment and on discretionary spending — Key risks named by management include dependence on the fine dining segment and a prolonged demand slowdown affecting discretionary dining, in a business whose leadership position is concentrated in the fine dining category.
- Geographic concentration of the network — Of 121 units as on March 31, 2026, Mumbai accounts for 49 and Kolkata 31, with the remainder thinly spread across Pune (11), Bangalore (12), Chennai (6), NCR (4), Ranchi (3), Hyderabad (2), Bhubaneswar (2), Chandigarh (1) and one each in London, Dubai and Oman, so city-level demand, regulation or property shocks carry disproportionate weight. Management separately flags geopolitical tensions affecting international operations or supply chains.
- High real estate and rental costs, and site-selection risk — High rentals in prime locations affect the economics of expansion, alongside reverse-charge GST on commercial leases. The risk register separately flags the risk of selecting non-profitable or non-feasible new locations, mitigated by a standardised feasibility study before every go / no-go decision.
- Talent shortage, attrition and succession — A majority of organised operators report shortages of trained kitchen and service staff; attracting, training and retaining skilled manpower remains a structural industry challenge. The risk register lists high attrition and ineffective succession planning, mitigated through defined career paths, a performance management and reward process, and systematic review of positions requiring succession plans.
- Intensifying competition and dependence on aggregator platforms — Competition is intensifying from global chains, well-funded domestic formats, cloud-first brands and the entry of quick-commerce platforms into prepared foods, while growth in delivery brings dependence on aggregator economics, including commission structures and control over customer data.
- Regulatory change and compliance complexity — Exposures include judicial restrictions on the levy of service charge (which impacted industry realisations from Q1 FY 2025-26), GST at 5% without input tax credit, evolving labour codes, and food safety and licensing requirements. The risk register cites complex and frequently changing regulation, mitigated by ongoing staff training, legal consultation, documentation and internal audits, and compliance-management software with workflow and ownership.
- Food safety, hygiene and waste management — A BRSR material issue: poor waste management in food service establishments can cause hygiene and sanitation problems and raise the likelihood of foodborne contamination. Mitigations include strict protocols for disposal of used cooking oil to an authorised biofuel manufacturer recognised by the Central Pollution Control Board, removal of confectioneries from shelves well before expiry for safe disposal, and management of process and end-of-life product wastes; supply chain checks include verifying vendor certifications for quality and ethical sourcing.

business.body:
- The deck's stated USP is the presence of its brands in multiple formats ranging from Fine Dining, Casual Dining, Resto Bar, Cloud kitchens and Confectioneries, on a claim to 'continue to dominate with our market leadership in the Pan-Asian/ Oriental cuisine segment'.
- Revenue is concentrated in the Oriental flagship pair: Mainland China at 22.4% and Asia Kitchen at 18.3% of Q1FY27 brand-wise revenue, with Oh! Calcutta at 12.4% (standalone, excluding outdoor catering, royalty income and other operating revenues).
- Brand portfolio is broad and stated to enjoy strong recall and customer loyalty, spanning Mainland China, Asia Kitchen by Mainland China, Oh! Calcutta, Sigree / Sigree Global Grill, Haka, Gong, Cafe Mezzuna, Siciliana, Riyasat, Flame & Grill, Hoppipola, Episode One, Jungle Safari, Walter's, Sweet Bengal, Dariole and a signature outdoor catering business.
- Company's journey slide: incorporated 1999 with two restaurants (Mainland China and Oh! Calcutta), raised private equity from SAIF Partners in 2007, IPO in 2012, network of 100 in 2014, first Dubai franchise in 2018, first London restaurant (Chourangi) in 2021, and a network of 118 restaurants, confectionaries and franchisees in 2026.

It serves dine-in guests as well as a growing delivery and takeaway channel through leading online food aggregators, which contributes approximately 27.74% of the sales mix. Alongside its Indian network it operates internationally through a capital-light franchise model in the Middle East and a joint-venture restaurant in London.

outlook.body: Revenue Growth: ~15% for FY27 (potential to exceed); Margin: Restaurant-level EBITDA 15-16% post-rent; Corporate costs reducing to 4% of revenue; Order Inflow: 32 new outlets planned (8 flagship, 15 Walters, 10 Sweet Bengal); Capex: INR 40 Cr total (INR 32 Cr for flagship, INR 5 Cr for QSR/confectionery, INR 1.12 Cr already spent on induction).

outlook.body: Pipeline of 32 new stores for FY27; Targeting 150 total touchpoints by March 2027 (from 121); Franchise model expanding with 6% royalty on top-line.
outlook.title: Order book & pipeline

outlook.body: Scaling Mainland China and Asia Kitchen to ~50 stores each over 5 years; Walters expanding to 20 stores with extended hours; Sweet Bengal rebranding + FMCG packaging launch; Franchise model for capital-light growth.
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Five stated priorities for FY 2026-27: guest experience and brand elevation; disciplined expansion; digital and operating intelligence; people and leadership; and responsible value creation
- Portfolio approach of nurturing the icon brands (Mainland China, Oh! Calcutta), scaling the proven growth engines (Asia Kitchen by Mainland China) and testing emerging concepts (GONG, Siciliana, Walters) with rigorous unit economics
- Disciplined expansion - scale priority brands across metros and selected high-potential cities, choosing locations carefully and favouring efficient formats, with progress measured by quality of each location, guest advocacy, resilience of restaurant economics and returns on every rupee invested rather than by outlet count
- Pivot to smaller and more efficient restaurant formats of around 2,000 sq. ft. that deliver faster breakeven, together with continuous brand renewal (brand refresh of Mainland China and Asia Kitchen by Mainland China)
- Capital-light international expansion, principally in the Middle East, through a franchise model requiring no capital expenditure from the Company while generating royalty-led earnings; Chourangi in London is operated under joint venture
- Franchising and asset-light expansion of established brands, particularly in Tier 2/3 cities and international markets
- Grow delivery and takeaway through aggregators, cloud kitchens, virtual brands and delivery-optimised menus, with eleven cloud kitchens already broadening reach
- Expansion of the fast-casual and QSR segment through Walters Burger to participate in the industry's fastest-growing categories while complementing premium offerings
- Digital and data-led operating intelligence applied to menu design, demand planning, loyalty, feedback and productivity; AI-driven analytics, CRM and contactless dining
- Mitigate kitchen fuel risk through PNG connectivity where available, selective adoption of induction and electric cooking equipment, multi-fuel contingency planning, energy-efficient kitchen design and menu engineering
- Leadership transition: appointment of Mr. Avik Chatterjee as Chief Executive Officer and Whole-Time Director for day-to-day execution, with the Chairman and Managing Director focusing on long-term strategy, governance and mentorship
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: During FY 2025-26 the Company opened nine new restaurants, including the launch of Asia Kitchen by Mainland China at Nexus Elante Mall, Chandigarh, extending its presence in Northern India. As at March 31, 2026 it had 121 restaurants (including 7 franchisees), 11 cloud kitchens and 40 confectionaries. Expansion is being executed through a pivot to smaller and more efficient restaurant formats of around 2,000 sq. ft. that deliver faster breakeven, with cloud kitchens used as a cost-effective, lower-capital-expenditure route to extend existing brands or launch delivery-first virtual brands (and as commissary kitchens that reduce rentals and optimise labour), and a kitchen-within-kitchen model that lets multiple cuisine brands operate from existing kitchen infrastructure with minimal incremental investment. Stated expansion avenues include Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities (faster breakeven, lower rentals), franchising and asset-light expansion of established brands, the fast-casual and QSR segment through Walters Burger, and collaborations with malls, airports, hotels and corporates. Internationally the Company expands through a capital-light franchise model that requires no capital expenditure from the Company while generating royalty-led earnings: building on Asia Kitchen by Mainland China at Burjuman Mall (Dubai) and the Mall of Oman (Muscat), a new outlet was launched at Deira City Centre, Dubai in March 2026, with openings at Abu Dhabi in the pipeline and an entry into Saudi Arabia and further UAE locations under active evaluation; timing of pipeline openings will be calibrated to conditions in the Gulf following the West Asia conflict. In the United Kingdom, Chourangi (London) is operated under joint venture. A separate call on capital is the kitchen energy transition: the accelerated shift to induction and electric cooking requires capital investment in equipment, electrical infrastructure and staff retraining.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Formalisation of Indian food services: Kearney and Swiggy project the market growing from about US$78 billion in 2025 to more than US$125 billion by 2030, with the organised segment contributing over 60% of incremental growth; NRAI estimates organised food services will grow at 13.2% annually through 2028
- Consumption tailwinds from policy - GST rationalisation and income tax relief have enhanced disposable incomes in the consuming classes that drive organised dining, boosting eating-out frequency and average spends
- Rising disposable income and a growing middle class driving premiumisation and demand for quality casual and fine dining
- Widening cuisine experimentation - consumers discovering more cuisines and brands, with regional Indian food regaining relevance alongside Korean, Vietnamese and Mexican cuisines, which plays to the Company's Pan-Asian strengths
- Dining-out growth beyond the top eight cities is accelerating; Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities offer faster breakeven, lower rentals and rapidly rising aspirations
- Delivery and takeaway now account for approximately 27.74% of relevant standalone sales, supported by aggregator partnerships and delivery-optimised menus; eleven cloud kitchens broaden reach
- Middle East is the most attractive near-term international market - affluent Indian and South Asian expatriate base, demand for Asian dining, mall and tourism infrastructure and superior returns on investment; the zero-capex franchise structure limits financial exposure to Gulf disruption
- Collaborations with malls, airports, hotels and corporates to access high-traffic, experience-led destinations, and leveraging festivals and cultural events to drive footfall
- Headwinds flagged: the West Asia war and Strait of Hormuz disruption raising gas and fuel costs and threatening supply continuity; kitchen energy transition costs; expected normalisation of input costs; high real estate and rental costs; talent shortage and attrition; intensifying competition including quick commerce; aggregator platform dependence; and regulatory change including judicial restrictions on service charge and GST at 5% without input tax credit
- Strategic pricing and customisation across locations, formats and customer segments to balance accessibility with profitability, alongside menu engineering as a cost lever
- International pipeline: a new Asia Kitchen by Mainland China outlet was launched at Deira City Centre, Dubai in March 2026, with openings at Abu Dhabi in the pipeline and an entry into Saudi Arabia and further UAE locations under active evaluation; the timing of pipeline openings will be calibrated to evolving regional conditions
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: SRL navigates input cost inflation via a strategic shift to electric induction cooking (78% complete) and initiates a store refresh cycle that lifted April SSG to 11.57% after a muted Q4 (2.25%). With INR 162 Cr cash reserves and a planned addition of 32 outlets in FY27, the company targets 15%+ revenue growth while maintaining a debt-free balance sheet.

currentContext.expansion: During FY 2025-26 the Company opened nine new restaurants, including the launch of Asia Kitchen by Mainland China at Nexus Elante Mall, Chandigarh, extending its presence in Northern India. As at March 31, 2026 it had 121 restaurants (including 7 franchisees), 11 cloud kitchens and 40 confectionaries. Expansion is being executed through a pivot to smaller and more efficient restaurant formats of around 2,000 sq. ft. that deliver faster breakeven, with cloud kitchens used as a cost-effective, lower-capital-expenditure route to extend existing brands or launch delivery-first virtual brands (and as commissary kitchens that reduce rentals and optimise labour), and a kitchen-within-kitchen model that lets multiple cuisine brands operate from existing kitchen infrastructure with minimal incremental investment. Stated expansion avenues include Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities (faster breakeven, lower rentals), franchising and asset-light expansion of established brands, the fast-casual and QSR segment through Walters Burger, and collaborations with malls, airports, hotels and corporates. Internationally the Company expands through a capital-light franchise model that requires no capital expenditure from the Company while generating royalty-led earnings: building on Asia Kitchen by Mainland China at Burjuman Mall (Dubai) and the Mall of Oman (Muscat), a new outlet was launched at Deira City Centre, Dubai in March 2026, with openings at Abu Dhabi in the pipeline and an entry into Saudi Arabia and further UAE locations under active evaluation; timing of pipeline openings will be calibrated to conditions in the Gulf following the West Asia conflict. In the United Kingdom, Chourangi (London) is operated under joint venture. A separate call on capital is the kitchen energy transition: the accelerated shift to induction and electric cooking requires capital investment in equipment, electrical infrastructure and staff retraining.

risks.risk: Kitchen fuel supply disruption and elevated gas and fuel prices
risks.note: Management names energy supply disruption and elevated gas and fuel prices arising from the West Asia conflict as a key risk, given the industry's dependence on LPG for commercial kitchens; curtailed LNG supplies have driven up gas and fuel prices, directly raising kitchen fuel costs, threatening supply continuity for gas-dependent operations and adding freight and imported-ingredient cost pressure, with the speed of restoration of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz named as a key variable to monitor. The Company mitigates this through PNG connectivity where available, selective adoption of induction and electric cooking equipment, multi-fuel contingency planning, energy-efficient kitchen design and menu engineering; energy management is also a BRSR material issue given reliance on refrigeration, air conditioning, lighting and LPG.

risks.risk: Cost of the kitchen energy transition
risks.note: The accelerated shift to induction and electric cooking requires capital investment in equipment, electrical infrastructure and staff retraining, and must be balanced against the flame-based techniques integral to the Company's cuisines.

risks.risk: Input cost volatility and inflation normalisation
risks.note: Food inflation was unusually amiable for most of FY 2025-26 but prices are expected to normalise, and the energy crisis has revived the risk of a resurgence in commodity, fuel, packaging and logistics costs that can compress margins. The risk register also flags commodity and material price fluctuation, mitigated by advance planning of commodity supplies and evaluating hedging for select commodities.

risks.risk: Dependence on the fine dining segment and on discretionary spending
risks.note: Key risks named by management include dependence on the fine dining segment and a prolonged demand slowdown affecting discretionary dining, in a business whose leadership position is concentrated in the fine dining category.

Of 121 units as on March 31, 2026, Mumbai accounts for 49 and Kolkata 31, with the remainder thinly spread across Pune (11), Bangalore (12), Chennai (6), NCR (4), Ranchi (3), Hyderabad (2), Bhubaneswar (2), Chandigarh (1) and one each in London, Dubai and Oman, so city-level demand, regulation or property shocks carry disproportionate weight. Management separately flags geopolitical tensions affecting international operations or supply chains.

risks.risk: High real estate and rental costs, and site-selection risk
risks.note: High rentals in prime locations affect the economics of expansion, alongside reverse-charge GST on commercial leases. The risk register separately flags the risk of selecting non-profitable or non-feasible new locations, mitigated by a standardised feasibility study before every go / no-go decision.

A majority of organised operators report shortages of trained kitchen and service staff; attracting, training and retaining skilled manpower remains a structural industry challenge. The risk register lists high attrition and ineffective succession planning, mitigated through defined career paths, a performance management and reward process, and systematic review of positions requiring succession plans.

risks.risk: Intensifying competition and dependence on aggregator platforms
risks.note: Competition is intensifying from global chains, well-funded domestic formats, cloud-first brands and the entry of quick-commerce platforms into prepared foods, while growth in delivery brings dependence on aggregator economics, including commission structures and control over customer data.

Exposures include judicial restrictions on the levy of service charge (which impacted industry realisations from Q1 FY 2025-26), GST at 5% without input tax credit, evolving labour codes, and food safety and licensing requirements. The risk register cites complex and frequently changing regulation, mitigated by ongoing staff training, legal consultation, documentation and internal audits, and compliance-management software with workflow and ownership.

risks.risk: Food safety, hygiene and waste management
risks.note: A BRSR material issue: poor waste management in food service establishments can cause hygiene and sanitation problems and raise the likelihood of foodborne contamination. Mitigations include strict protocols for disposal of used cooking oil to an authorised biofuel manufacturer recognised by the Central Pollution Control Board, removal of confectioneries from shelves well before expiry for safe disposal, and management of process and end-of-life product wastes; supply chain checks include verifying vendor certifications for quality and ethical sourcing.

one-line thesis: SRL navigates input cost inflation via a strategic shift to electric induction cooking (78% complete) and initiates a store refresh cycle that lifted April SSG to 11.57% after a muted Q4 (2.25%). With INR 162 Cr cash reserves and a planned addition of 32 outlets in FY27, the company targets 15%+ revenue growth while maintaining a debt-free balance sheet.
financial scorecard: Revenue: +13.65% YoY (Quarter); EBITDA Margin: Gross margin improved to 70.4% (from 69.1%); PAT: +44.20% YoY; Order Book: N/A (Retail); Net Debt: Net Cash of INR 103 Cr (Total Cash INR 162.48 Cr). One-offs: Significant capex on induction woks (INR 1.12 Cr) to mitigate fuel risk; No major accounting distortions noted.
guidance: Revenue Growth: ~15% for FY27 (potential to exceed); Margin: Restaurant-level EBITDA 15-16% post-rent; Corporate costs reducing to 4% of revenue; Order Inflow: 32 new outlets planned (8 flagship, 15 Walters, 10 Sweet Bengal); Capex: INR 40 Cr total (INR 32 Cr for flagship, INR 5 Cr for QSR/confectionery, INR 1.12 Cr already spent on induction).
order book & pipeline: Pipeline of 32 new stores for FY27; Targeting 150 total touchpoints by March 2027 (from 121); Franchise model expanding with 6% royalty on top-line.
segment / subsidiary detail: Focus brands: Mainland China, Asia Kitchen, Haka, Gong, Siciliana, Walters, Sweet Bengal. Non-focus brands paused for expansion but remain profitable. Gong (Premium) AOV INR 2,500-3,000; Mainland China AOV INR 1,200-1,300; Asia Kitchen AOV INR 1,000-1,100; Walters AOV INR 700; Sweet Bengal AOV INR 400.
growth verticals / optionality: Scaling Mainland China and Asia Kitchen to ~50 stores each over 5 years; Walters expanding to 20 stores with extended hours; Sweet Bengal rebranding + FMCG packaging launch; Franchise model for capital-light growth.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin 70.4%. Rental cost ~20-21% of revenue. Restaurant-level EBITDA 15% post-rent. Corporate costs amortizing down to 4% due to expansion. Induction cooking expected to save ~6% vs gas by eliminating pilot light wastage.
capex / expansion: FY27 Guidance: INR 40 Cr. Breakdown: INR 32 Cr for 8 new flagship restaurants; INR 5 Cr for QSR/confectionery; INR 1.12 Cr already incurred for induction wok conversion (300 sets imported).
capital allocation: Debt-free with INR 162.48 Cr cash (Net Cash INR 103 Cr). No confirmed buyback yet; Board to consider based on cash flow utilization. Reinvestment prioritized for store refreshes and new openings.
risks & watch-items: Input cost inflation (fuel, freight); Consumer discretionary spend compression; Execution risk on store refreshes; Geopolitical uncertainty impacting global supply chains (mentioned 'Trump behavior').
management quality / tone: Cautiously optimistic; Operationally agile (rapid induction shift); Confident in brand equity; Prudent on pricing (only 4% hike passed to customers).
non-obvious takeaways: 78% of chain converted to electric induction woks in <2 months to hedge against LPG/PNG scarcity; Pilot testing shows 6% cost saving vs gas due to elimination of 'pilot light' wastage; April SSG surged to 11.57% immediately following store refreshes, validating the renovation thesis.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Speciality Restaurants Limited is a multi-brand Indian food-services company with a leadership position in fine dining, operating 121 restaurants along with cloud kitchens and confectioneries as at March 31, 2026.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company owns and operates a portfolio of restaurant and confectionery brands across multiple formats - Fine Dining, Casual Dining, Resto Bars, QSR (Quick Service Restaurants) and Cloud Kitchens to Confectioneries - built on Pan-Asian/Oriental and regional Indian culinary expertise developed over three decades. It serves dine-in guests as well as a growing delivery and takeaway channel through leading online food aggregators, which contributes approximately 27.74% of the sales mix. Alongside its Indian network it operates internationally through a capital-light franchise model in the Middle East and a joint-venture restaurant in London.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Formalisation of Indian food services: Kearney and Swiggy project the market growing from about US$78 billion in 2025 to more than US$125 billion by 2030, with the organised segment contributing over 60% of incremental growth; NRAI estimates organised food services will grow at 13.2% annually through 2028
- Consumption tailwinds from policy - GST rationalisation and income tax relief have enhanced disposable incomes in the consuming classes that drive organised dining, boosting eating-out frequency and average spends
- Rising disposable income and a growing middle class driving premiumisation and demand for quality casual and fine dining
- Widening cuisine experimentation - consumers discovering more cuisines and brands, with regional Indian food regaining relevance alongside Korean, Vietnamese and Mexican cuisines, which plays to the Company's Pan-Asian strengths
- Dining-out growth beyond the top eight cities is accelerating; Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities offer faster breakeven, lower rentals and rapidly rising aspirations
- Delivery and takeaway now account for approximately 27.74% of relevant standalone sales, supported by aggregator partnerships and delivery-optimised menus; eleven cloud kitchens broaden reach
- Middle East is the most attractive near-term international market - affluent Indian and South Asian expatriate base, demand for Asian dining, mall and tourism infrastructure and superior returns on investment; the zero-capex franchise structure limits financial exposure to Gulf disruption
- Collaborations with malls, airports, hotels and corporates to access high-traffic, experience-led destinations, and leveraging festivals and cultural events to drive footfall
- Headwinds flagged: the West Asia war and Strait of Hormuz disruption raising gas and fuel costs and threatening supply continuity; kitchen energy transition costs; expected normalisation of input costs; high real estate and rental costs; talent shortage and attrition; intensifying competition including quick commerce; aggregator platform dependence; and regulatory change including judicial restrictions on service charge and GST at 5% without input tax credit
- Strategic pricing and customisation across locations, formats and customer segments to balance accessibility with profitability, alongside menu engineering as a cost lever
- International pipeline: a new Asia Kitchen by Mainland China outlet was launched at Deira City Centre, Dubai in March 2026, with openings at Abu Dhabi in the pipeline and an entry into Saudi Arabia and further UAE locations under active evaluation; the timing of pipeline openings will be calibrated to evolving regional conditions

- Nineteenth consecutive quarter of sustained profitable growth in FY 2025-26

- Capital-light international franchise model that requires no capital expenditure from the Company while generating royalty-led earnings and limiting financial exposure to regional disruption
- Debt-free position and brand strength described as meaningful advantages in a period of elevated gas, fuel and input costs
- Growing delivery franchise supported by strategic partnerships with leading online food aggregators and delivery-optimised menus
- Brand recognition through awards during the year for Mainland China, Asia Kitchen by Mainland China, Oh! Calcutta, Sigree, Riyasat, Café Mezzuna and Sweet Bengal

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:

one-line thesis: SRL navigates input cost inflation via a strategic shift to electric induction cooking (78% complete) and initiates a store refresh cycle that lifted April SSG to 11.57% after a muted Q4 (2.25%). With INR 162 Cr cash reserves and a planned addition of 32 outlets in FY27, the company targets 15%+ revenue growth while maintaining a debt-free balance sheet.

One-offs: Significant capex on induction woks (INR 1.12 Cr) to mitigate fuel risk; No major accounting distortions noted.
guidance: Revenue Growth: ~15% for FY27 (potential to exceed); Margin: Restaurant-level EBITDA 15-16% post-rent; Corporate costs reducing to 4% of revenue; Order Inflow: 32 new outlets planned (8 flagship, 15 Walters, 10 Sweet Bengal); Capex: INR 40 Cr total (INR 32 Cr for flagship, INR 5 Cr for QSR/confectionery, INR 1.12 Cr already spent on induction).
order book & pipeline: Pipeline of 32 new stores for FY27; Targeting 150 total touchpoints by March 2027 (from 121); Franchise model expanding with 6% royalty on top-line.
segment / subsidiary detail: Focus brands: Mainland China, Asia Kitchen, Haka, Gong, Siciliana, Walters, Sweet Bengal. Non-focus brands paused for expansion but remain profitable. Gong (Premium) AOV INR 2,500-3,000; Mainland China AOV INR 1,200-1,300; Asia Kitchen AOV INR 1,000-1,100; Walters AOV INR 700; Sweet Bengal AOV INR 400.
growth verticals / optionality: Scaling Mainland China and Asia Kitchen to ~50 stores each over 5 years; Walters expanding to 20 stores with extended hours; Sweet Bengal rebranding + FMCG packaging launch; Franchise model for capital-light growth.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin 70.4%. Rental cost ~20-21% of revenue. Restaurant-level EBITDA 15% post-rent. Corporate costs amortizing down to 4% due to expansion. Induction cooking expected to save ~6% vs gas by eliminating pilot light wastage.
capex / expansion: FY27 Guidance: INR 40 Cr. Breakdown: INR 32 Cr for 8 new flagship restaurants; INR 5 Cr for QSR/confectionery; INR 1.12 Cr already incurred for induction wok conversion (300 sets imported).
capital allocation: Debt-free with INR 162.48 Cr cash (Net Cash INR 103 Cr). No confirmed buyback yet; Board to consider based on cash flow utilization. Reinvestment prioritized for store refreshes and new openings.

management quality / tone: Cautiously optimistic; Operationally agile (rapid induction shift); Confident in brand equity; Prudent on pricing (only 4% hike passed to customers).
